1.name: Léandre Charbonneau
1.about: Already carrying No. 1 pick expectations entering the year, Charbonneau did little to loosen his grip on the top spot. Against professionals in Perth, the French teenager flashed explosive finishing, confident perimeter shooting and multi-positional defense. Size, length, athleticism and legitimate two-way upside continue to distinguish him from an otherwise talented class.

2.name: Awut Jok
2.about: A dominant freshman campaign has pushed Jok firmly into the No. 2 spot on draft boards. Duke’s towering center controlled the glass, protected the rim and displayed increasingly convincing shooting touch throughout the season. Despite limited athleticism, his production, enormous dimensions and rapid development have strengthened the belief that his ceiling extends well beyond his current game.

3.name: Zhaire Jefferson
3.about: Jefferson backed up his elite prospect status with one of the strongest freshman seasons in the class, combining explosive downhill creation with advanced scoring touch inside the arc. His 6'9" wingspan gives him intriguing defensive potential, while his ability to consistently create advantages off the dribble has solidified him as a legitimate top-three prospect.

4.name: Dremonte Johnson Jr.
4.about: Few players in college basketball could match the sheer physical impact Johnson brought to Michigan’s frontcourt. His sophomore season featured violent finishes, dominant stretches around the rim and increasingly intimidating defense. Already an elite athlete with exceptional length and power, further shooting development could unlock another dimension for one of the class’ premier prospects.

5.name: Nate Johnson
5.about: A 17.8-point freshman campaign has Johnson firmly positioned as a top-five pick. The 6'8" Alabama scorer showcased advanced pull-up ability, comfortable shot creation and the size to attack a variety of matchups. Questions remain defensively and as a playmaker, but his polished three-level scoring gives him one of the class’ highest offensive ceilings.

6.name: Michael Cheeks
6.about: Cheeks entered the season projected inside the top two, but an inefficient freshman campaign caused his stock to settle at No. 6. The shot-making flashes remained impressive, particularly off the dribble and from deep, but questionable shot selection and inconsistent finishing hurt his efficiency. Despite the slide, his size and scoring talent still give him considerable upside.

7.name: Branko Simić
7.about: No prospect climbed draft boards more dramatically this season than Simić. The 6'10" Serbian wing emerged as a legitimate lottery talent, using exceptional length to erase shots and create defensive disruption while flashing increasingly dangerous downhill scoring. His jumper remains inconsistent, but rapid development and unusual two-way tools have transformed his NBA outlook.

8.name: Hashim Newman
8.about: Producing like a featured scorer while maintaining legitimate two-way value propelled Newman firmly into the lottery conversation. The Santa Clara sophomore punished defenses from the perimeter, competed physically and remained active defensively. Self-creation is still developing, but his combination of shooting, strength and production gives teams an appealing foundation to build around.

9.name: Danny Reich
9.about: Reich has been one of college basketball's biggest risers, going from barely appearing on preseason draft boards to a projected top-10 pick. His elite shooting, playmaking feel and 6'6" size have driven the ascent, while his relentless intensity consistently shows on both ends. Limited explosiveness remains his biggest physical question entering the NBA.

10.name: Izaiah Battle
10.about: Battle emerged as one of the class’s premier freshman scorers, using his powerful 220-pound frame to consistently bully his way into the paint and create quality looks inside the arc. His combination of strength, midrange shot-making and contact finishing gives him a distinctive scoring profile, establishing him firmly as a projected top-10 pick.

11.name: Kevin Carter
11.about: Carter’s freshman numbers hardly resemble those of a typical lottery pick, but NBA teams remain enamored with the tools. At 6'9" with a 7'3" wingspan, he flashed explosive transition finishing, disruptive defensive potential and stretches of dynamic slashing at Kansas. Developing his jumper and half-court skill will determine whether those flashes become consistent production.

12.name: Josh Houston
12.about: Immediate energy around the basket allowed Houston to carve out an important role during his lone season at North Carolina. The freshman sprinted the floor, attacked the offensive glass and finished emphatically while providing useful defensive activity. His offensive repertoire remains narrow, though his length, strength and athleticism provide a straightforward NBA pathway.

13.name: Asafa Tinibu
13.about: Once considered a top-five prospect, Tinibu has slipped to No. 13 as concerns surrounding his perimeter game have grown. His explosive first step, powerful rim attacks and enormous 6'11" wingspan still give him one of the class’s more enticing physical profiles. Improving his jumper and expanding his half-court creation will be critical to maximizing that upside.

14.name: Jake Jones
14.about: Few freshman bigs provided more immediate interior reliability than Jones did at Texas. His combination of vertical athleticism, length and timing translated into efficient finishes and consistent paint protection, giving him a clear NBA role. The skill game remains fairly basic, but his physical tools have solidified him as a mid-first-round prospect.

15.name: Borja Barbero
15.about: Barbero has steadily strengthened his first-round case against professional competition, offering an appealing blend of positional size, creativity and scoring touch. At 6'6", he sees passing windows over smaller guards and is comfortable creating from the midrange. His versatility is enticing, though inconsistent three-point shooting and decision-making keep him outside the lottery.

16.name: Jan Zorko
16.about: Once discussed as a possible top-10 selection, Zorko watched his stock cool during an uneven year with Cedevita Olimpija. Flashes of grab-and-go playmaking and instinctive defense remain enticing, but limited production exposed how far his scoring still has to develop. At only 19, his unusual versatility preserves considerable first-round intrigue.

17.name: Sabian Jefferson
17.about: Widely regarded as the best shooter in the class, Jefferson shot himself into the top 20 with a brilliant senior season at St. John's. His deep range, rapid release and pull-up shot-making force defenses to account for him well beyond the arc. His offensive gravity is undeniable, though limited size and athleticism create real defensive and finishing concerns.

18.name: Gunnar Davies
18.about: One season at Duke was enough for Davies to establish himself as one of the draft’s premier shooters. The Australian junior averaged 18.3 points behind elite perimeter shot-making, thriving off movement and comfortably creating jumpers off the bounce. Limited athleticism and defensive upside cap his ceiling, but his shooting gives him immediate NBA value.

19.name: Aaron Kelly
19.about: A former five-star and highly ranked recruit, Kelly arrived at Arkansas with significant expectations and quickly showed why scouts valued his offensive polish. His change of pace, handle and touch allow him to consistently manufacture looks inside the arc. His freshman production has kept him firmly in first-round territory, although average athleticism and defensive limitations temper his ceiling.

20.name: Terry Davidson Jr.
20.about: Davidson’s combination of 6'7" size and a 7'0" wingspan immediately separated him from most freshman wings, helping him emerge as a top-20 prospect. He thrives attacking gaps, finishing in transition and using his length defensively. His physical tools offer clear two-way upside, though his jumper and self-creation remain works in progress.

21.name: Jaxson Woods
21.about: A former five-star recruit, Woods arrived at Memphis with major expectations and delivered a productive freshman season as a primary creator. His advanced handle, change of pace and pull-up game consistently created offense, while his passing showed legitimate lead-guard potential. Questions surrounding his size, finishing and average athleticism have kept him just outside the top 20.

22.name: Braylon Farmer
22.about: A major sophomore scoring leap transformed Farmer into a clear first-round prospect. The left-handed wing averaged 18.1 points behind smooth pull-up shooting and aggressive downhill attacks, using his length to finish over smaller defenders. His efficiency and decision-making can fluctuate, but the combination of size, scoring versatility and creation gives him legitimate upside.

23.name: Tyler Hawkins
23.about: A former four-star recruit, Hawkins exceeded expectations during his freshman season and developed into a legitimate first-round prospect. His 6'5" frame, massive 6'11" wingspan, dependable shooting and disruptive perimeter defense give him an easy NBA role. Expanding his handle and self-creation will determine whether he develops into more than a high-level complementary guard.

24.name: Taevion Bryant
24.about: Bryant's defensive dominance became the foundation of his rise into the first round, as he established himself as the best defender in the class. His relentless ball pressure, physicality and 6'7" wingspan allow him to overwhelm opposing guards and generate turnovers. His offensive game remains less polished, with inconsistent shooting limiting his effectiveness away from the ball.

25.name: Jonah Middleton
25.about: Two seasons at Georgia Tech preceded a move to Gonzaga that ultimately helped Middleton establish his NBA case. By his senior year, the 6'8" forward had become a polished floor spacer and intelligent connective passer. Athletic and defensive limitations cap his upside, but his offensive versatility provides a compelling late-first-round argument.

26.name: Niko Vincetić
26.about: Rebounding instincts and floor-spacing potential became Vincetić’s calling cards during his season with Cibona. Despite standing only 6'8", the Croatian forward consistently competed above his size on the glass while developing into a credible perimeter threat. Questions surrounding athleticism and defensive range make identifying his ideal NBA matchup considerably more difficult.

27.name: Tyler McCoy
27.about: Defense became McCoy’s calling card during an encouraging freshman season at Ohio State. He rarely commanded offensive touches, instead making his impact through disciplined positioning, rebounding and consistent rim deterrence. His 7'4" wingspan compensates for average athleticism, although a limited scoring arsenal leaves teams projecting him primarily as a defensive-minded NBA center.

28.name: Antoine Dupont
28.about: Defense drove Dupont’s rise despite limited minutes with JL Bourg. His 7'5" wingspan, quick reactions and impressive mobility produced intriguing flashes both protecting the rim and defending away from the basket. He remains physically underdeveloped and largely unproven, but his potential to eventually anchor a versatile NBA defense has secured first-round interest.

29.name: Justinas Jakčinskas
29.about: Arriving from Lithuania before beginning his college career, Jakčinskas developed into Arkansas’ defensive tone-setter as a sophomore. His combination of size, physicality and quick reactions made him particularly disruptive around the basket, while his relentless motor consistently created second-effort plays. Offensive limitations remain substantial, making his defense the foundation of his NBA projection.

30.name: Terrell Lewis
30.about: College basketball’s Player of the Year enters the draft after a spectacular 23.2-point senior season at Purdue. Lewis established himself as one of the nation’s premier scorers, combining high-volume perimeter shooting with exceptional off-ball movement and deep range. Questions about athleticism and creation remain, making his NBA ceiling less certain than his decorated résumé suggests.

31.name: Isaiah McGee
31.about: McGee’s freshman season was more about flashes than sustained production. The Gonzaga wing showed intriguing isolation shot-making, a confident perimeter jumper and enough length to bother opposing scorers despite modest athleticism. His consistency and ability to create separation remain developmental, but a two-way skill foundation at only 19 gives teams reason to remain patient.

32.name: Ashton Howard
32.about: Howard carved out a first-round profile at Kentucky by embracing a complementary role, providing reliable perimeter shooting, length and disciplined defense rather than dominating the ball. His 6'10" wingspan gives him legitimate multi-position defensive potential, while his spot-up shooting translates cleanly. Questions remain about his handle and ability to consistently create offense himself.

33.name: Nigel Butler Jr.
33.about: A breakout 19.1-point junior campaign turned Butler into one of UCLA’s most impactful two-way players. Physical drives and opportunistic transition scoring fueled his offense, while aggressive hands and anticipation consistently created turnovers defensively. His production warrants NBA attention, but an unreliable perimeter jumper remains the biggest reason he sits outside the first round.

34.name: Xavion Booker
34.about: Booker arrived at USC following a legendary high school career and entered the season surrounded by significant draft buzz, but that excitement cooled as his freshman year progressed. His handle and pull-up creation still produced enticing flashes, though inconsistent shooting and efficiency exposed areas of needed development and pushed him toward the early-second-round range.

35.name: Leopoldo Santamaría
35.about: Production tells only part of the story with Santamaría, whose limited Olimpia Milano role still contained intriguing offensive flashes. Soft touch, patient footwork and promising passing instincts stood out whenever opportunities arrived. His average physical tools leave plenty to prove, but teams remain interested in the Spanish forward’s feel and developmental scoring potential.

36.name: Jalen Hurd
36.about: Arriving at Michigan State as a five-star, top-13 national recruit, Hurd entered college with significant NBA expectations. An 8.6-point freshman season exposed how raw his offensive game remains, though explosive slashing and defensive flashes preserved his draft appeal. Inconsistent shooting and creation have hurt his stock, leaving teams to bet primarily on his physical upside.

37.name: Ian Hopkins
37.about: Once a prized Duke recruit, Hopkins’ winding college career included one season in Durham and two at St. John’s before a final stop at UCLA. The powerful senior finally found stability, turning his strength and explosiveness into consistent downhill production. His circuitous development raises questions, but the physical tools remain clearly NBA-caliber.

38.name: Cameron Bryan
38.about: Nearly 20 points per game made Bryan one of the most productive senior forwards in the class. Sacramento State leaned heavily on his strength, shooting touch and versatile scoring throughout the year. That production is difficult to ignore, although his age, level of competition and uncertain defensive position prevent scouts from viewing him as a first-round certainty.

39.name: Rayshawn Bernard
39.about: Bernard carved out his draft stock through physicality, explosive finishing and relentless point-of-attack defense. His powerful 218-pound frame and 6'9" wingspan allow him to overwhelm smaller guards and defend bigger wings, while his athleticism generates havoc in transition. The major concern remains his jumper, which limits his effectiveness when forced away from the rim.

40.name: Christian Dillon
40.about: Auburn frequently trusted Dillon to organize offense from the elbows and low post, where his passing became the defining feature of his sophomore season. He sees cutters early, makes quick reads and scores with touch inside. Questions surrounding his shooting, athleticism and defensive ceiling push an otherwise unusual offensive skill set into second-round territory.

41.name: Kris Sanders
41.about: Four college seasons have shaped Sanders into a fairly straightforward NBA projection: defend wings, space the floor and play within the offense. His 7'0" wingspan gives him useful matchup versatility, while improved spot-up shooting has made him more functional off the ball. Limited creation lowers the ceiling, but his complementary skill set offers second-round value.

42.name: Noah Wunungmurra
42.about: Wunungmurra earned second-round attention with his physical guard play and defensive tools against professional competition in Australia. His 6'10" wingspan allows him to pressure ball-handlers and disrupt passing lanes, while his strength and burst help him attack downhill. His half-court creation remains inconsistent, and developing a more dependable jumper will be important for his NBA translation.

43.name: Andrew Bryant
43.about: Bryant’s unusual blend of wing size and perimeter finesse makes him an intriguing second-round scorer. At 6'9", the Texas junior uses change-of-pace moves and a smooth jumper to create shots without relying on explosiveness. His slender frame and average athleticism create defensive concerns, but shooting and positional size give his offensive game NBA potential.

44.name: Marquise Farmer
44.about: A polished scoring season at Liberty put Farmer firmly on the NBA radar. The 257-pound junior did his best work from the mid-post, combining strength with soft touch, patient footwork and enough shooting ability to punish defenses outside the paint. Defensive limitations and average athleticism complicate his projection, but his scoring craft gives him second-round appeal.

45.name: Kaiden Wilson
45.about: Explosive drives and comfortable pull-up shooting offered glimpses of something more during Wilson’s uneven sophomore campaign. Illinois never received that version consistently, with unreliable three-point shooting and limited creation preventing a larger breakout. The physical tools remain appealing, but his undefined offensive role has pushed the athletic forward into the middle-second-round range.

46.name: Keifon Jackson
46.about: Jackson remains an intriguing developmental prospect because of his 6'7" frame, 7'0" wingspan and flashes of two-way athleticism. His freshman production was limited, but he showed enough defensive versatility and transition finishing to maintain second-round interest. The offensive skill set remains raw, particularly as a shooter and self-creator.

47.name: Julien Watson
47.about: Few players in the class carried a heavier scoring burden than Watson, who erupted for 23.6 points per game during his junior season at Oregon. His movement shooting, quick release and ability to manufacture difficult jumpers made him an elite college scorer. Poor athleticism, limited length and defensive concerns explain why that production hasn’t translated into first-round positioning.

48.name: Ivan Vesić
48.about: Vesić offers one of the more unusual guard profiles in the second round, combining 6'7" size and a 6'11" wingspan with impressive open-floor finishing and above-the-rim athleticism. His professional role remained relatively limited, but flashes of transition playmaking and defensive versatility keep scouts interested in his developmental upside.

49.name: Pip Richardson
49.about: Playing on a stacked Michigan roster filled with NBA-caliber talent, Richardson ultimately proved to be the team's unquestioned leader. His shooting, steady playmaking and command of the offense consistently kept Michigan organized in big moments. His experience and competitiveness are major selling points, though his age, limited athleticism and defensive ceiling restrict his long-term upside.

50.name: Tristen Gaines
50.about: There is little mystery surrounding what Gaines could provide an NBA roster. Colorado’s senior forward spaced the floor, defended within the team structure and contributed without demanding touches. His average athletic profile and limited creation restrict the upside, but a dependable combination of shooting and defensive competence keeps him squarely in second-round consideration.

51.name: Berkay Şimşek
51.about: Şimşek earned legitimate draft consideration through his mature approach against professional competition, showing patience operating out of ball screens and impressive touch inside the arc. He rarely overwhelms defenders physically, instead relying on pace, footwork and feel to create offense. His limited burst and defensive ceiling leave him projected near the second-round bubble.

52.name: Cheikh Tidiane Mbodj
52.about: NBA interest in Mbodj is driven far more by projection than his limited production for Real Madrid. The 19-year-old Senegalese forward combines a 7'2" wingspan with impressive vertical pop, flashing weak-side rim protection and switchable defensive potential. His offensive game remains extremely raw, positioning him as a developmental undrafted prospect with intriguing physical tools.

53.name: Jeremy Conway
53.about: Conway turned four years of college experience into a well-rounded senior season, providing Villanova with steady scoring, secondary creation and dependable perimeter play. He lacks a single standout NBA trait, but his size, shooting and decision-making give him a pathway as a reliable reserve guard. At 22, teams will weigh his polish against limited upside.

54.name: Kaysan Williams
54.about: Playmaking at 6'8" is the skill keeping Williams in the draft conversation. UConn regularly placed the ball in the junior wing’s hands, allowing him to initiate offense, manipulate defenders and create for teammates while mixing in a developing scoring package. Inconsistent shooting and average athleticism limit his margin for error as an NBA creator.

55.name: Kaprice Jackson
55.about: Open space is where Jackson makes his strongest NBA argument. The Arkansas junior excels attacking gaps, running the floor and turning defensive breakdowns into quick scoring opportunities, while an improving jumper gives him some complementary value. Without standout length or advanced creation ability, however, his path to an NBA role remains relatively narrow.

56.name: Ryan Hurley
56.about: Hurley built his draft case around an unusual combination of wing size, shooting and passing feel, becoming the engine of Belmont’s offense as a senior. He consistently punished defenses as a spot-up threat and connective playmaker, but his lack of athleticism raises significant questions about separation, finishing and his ability to survive defensively at the NBA level.

57.name: Nelson Esteva
57.about: Versatility rather than traditional center play defined Esteva’s senior year at UC Irvine. The Spanish-American forward-center comfortably switched onto guards, absorbed contact against bigger players and generated turnovers with active hands. He lacks ideal length and rim-protection ability for the five, but his strength and perimeter defense could translate into a valuable situational NBA role.

58.name: Andy Enriquez
58.about: Enriquez developed into a tough two-way guard at Seton Hall, using a strong frame, advanced handle and impressive 6'7" wingspan to impact both ends. He can create advantages off the dribble and bother opposing ball-handlers defensively, but his inconsistent jumper limits his spacing value. He enters the draft firmly on the second-round bubble.

59.name: Bellamy Nichols
59.about: Nichols is one of the draft's most physically unusual guards, packing 215 pounds and explosive leaping ability into a 6'0" frame. His strength and burst create spectacular finishes and allow him to pressure the rim despite his height. The athletic tools are undeniable, but questionable shooting, playmaking and positional size leave him on the draft bubble.

60.name: Jayden Bonds
60.about: Bonds showed enough shot-making and on-ball creativity during his freshman season at UCLA to keep himself in the draft conversation. He is comfortable creating pull-up jumpers and navigating ball screens, but his impact fluctuated throughout the year. With average physical tools and limited size, teams will want more consistency as a shooter and playmaker.

61.name: Zaquan Simms
61.about: Three seasons at Michigan State preceded Simms’ transfer to Kentucky, where he spent his senior year settling into a complementary role. Transition activity, purposeful cutting and defensive effort provided steady value, but his jumper never became consistent enough to elevate his NBA stock. Without a standout offensive skill, he enters the process as an undrafted candidate.

62.name: Fiachra O’Loingsigh
62.about: Size alone makes O’Loingsigh difficult to ignore. The 7'3" Irish center saw limited action for Olympiacos, but his enormous reach produced imposing rim-protection flashes whenever opportunities arrived. Severe mobility and offensive limitations make his NBA fit increasingly difficult, leaving teams to decide whether his paint presence warrants a developmental or two-way opportunity.

63.name: Terryl Wiley
63.about: Wiley was one of college basketball's most productive senior scorers, carrying Saint Louis with his pull-up jumper, crafty left-handed handle and relentless shot creation. His scoring production demands attention, but scouts remain skeptical about how it translates against NBA size and athleticism. At 6'1", his defense and finishing limitations leave him projected outside the draft.

64.name: Nisini Omondumuhi
64.about: Being only 21 after four college seasons gives Omondumuhi more developmental runway than the typical senior prospect. South Carolina regularly trusted his length and quickness against challenging perimeter assignments, where his defensive value was obvious. Offensively, however, little progress materialized, leaving the Nigerian forward projected as an undrafted two-way candidate.

65.name: Brendan Garza
65.about: Garza was a productive sophomore guard for Purdue, showing advanced pick-and-roll feel, shooting touch and an ability to organize offense in the half court. His skill level keeps him on the NBA radar, but a limited physical profile and poor athletic tools create significant concerns about his ability to separate, finish and defend against NBA guards.

66.name: Angus Bryant
66.about: Bryant built his professional résumé around aggressive perimeter scoring and disruptive defense, flashing the confidence to create his own jumper against experienced competition. His shooting and active hands provide a potential NBA niche, but at 6'2" with modest length and limited explosiveness, his size makes translating his combo-guard game to the next level difficult.

67.name: John Miller
67.about: A productive senior campaign at North Dakota State showcased Miller’s ability to impose himself physically around the basket. Strength, rebounding and interior finishing generated consistent results, but his game remains overwhelmingly paint-oriented. Without dependable shooting or perimeter skill to broaden his role, scouts currently view his production as more attractive for undrafted free agency than draft night.

68.name: Adrian Evans
68.about: Four years at Purdue have turned Evans into a dependable, physical college center, but at 24, scouts question how much development remains. He rebounds, establishes deep position and competes defensively without requiring touches. His lack of shooting and athleticism significantly narrow his NBA role, placing him firmly in the undrafted free-agent conversation.

69.name: Hunter Heckmann
69.about: Elite shooting is Heckman’s clearest path toward overcoming a difficult NBA athletic profile. Oregon’s senior wing consistently created value through movement, quick-trigger threes and intelligent relocation, giving defenses little room to lose track of him. With poor athleticism and limited defensive tools, however, he enters the process as an undrafted specialist candidate.

70.name: Luke Ashley
70.about: Offensive feel gives Ashley a more interesting résumé than his No. 69 ranking might suggest. The 6'8" junior functioned as a secondary creator for Creighton, pairing accurate perimeter shooting with advanced passing reads and positional size. Poor athleticism and limited defensive tools remain significant concerns, leaving him projected for undrafted free agency despite his offensive versatility.

71.name: Darrell Bernard
71.about: Double-digit rebounding and relentless interior work defined Bernard’s final season at Notre Dame. The powerful senior consistently created extra possessions, finished through contact and imposed himself physically around the basket. His college effectiveness is undeniable, but being a 23-year-old undersized non-shooter makes finding a sustainable NBA frontcourt role considerably more difficult.

72.name: Joey Owens
72.about: Owens became Wofford’s primary perimeter scorer as a senior, relying on crafty footwork, change of pace and a polished jumper to manufacture offense. His ability to hit difficult shots gives him a potential scoring niche, but limited burst, size and defensive tools make his NBA translation uncertain and leave him fighting for an opportunity after the draft.

73.name: Jaden Walker
73.about: Rebounding and old-school interior work powered Walker through a productive junior season at Gonzaga. He carved out space with his 251-pound frame, generated second chances and showed dependable touch around the basket. NBA questions center on everything outside the paint, as limited mobility, shooting and defensive range leave him fighting for a draft-day selection.

74.name: Devin Little
74.about: Still only 19 after completing his sophomore season, Little is one of the youngest players sitting near the bottom of the board. His 6'8" frame, open-floor speed and flashes of downhill finishing offer developmental intrigue, but an inconsistent jumper and limited half-court creation remain substantial hurdles. He projects as a priority undrafted developmental prospect.

75.name: Johnny Randall
75.about: At 6'6" and 245 pounds, Randall has built his entire game around winning physical battles against larger opponents. The Wisconsin junior attacks the glass, generates second chances and finishes through contact with relentless effort. Those qualities earn attention, but severe shooting, size and rim-protection limitations make his professional positional fit extremely difficult to solve.
